title: SYNDACTYLY, TYPE III
alt_titles: SYNDACTYLY OF FINGERS IV AND V

intro.text: This entry describes syndactyly type III (SDTY3). Type III syndactyly is also a characteristic feature of oculodentodigital dysplasia, which is caused by mutation in the gene encoding connexin-43 (GJA1; 121014) on chromosome 6q22.31 (Brueton et al., 1990; Paznekas et al., 2003).

checks.claim: Type III syndactyly is a characteristic feature of oculodentodigital dysplasia.
checks.evidence_quote: Syndactyly type III and conductive deafness can occur in some cases, and cardiac abnormalities are observed in rare instances.
checks.explanation: The abstract links syndactyly type III to ODDD but says it 'can occur in some cases', which is weaker than calling it a characteristic feature.

checks.claim: Oculodentodigital dysplasia is caused by mutation in the gene encoding connexin-43 (GJA1).
checks.evidence_quote: We found mutations in the GJA1 gene in all 17 families with oculodentodigital dysplasia that we screened.
checks.explanation: The title and abstract state that GJA1 (connexin 43) mutations cause ODDD.

checks.claim: The GJA1 gene, which encodes connexin-43, is located on chromosome 6q22.31.
checks.evidence_quote: The human connexin 43 gene, or GJA1, is located at human chromosome 6q22-q23 within the candidate region for the oculodentodigital dysplasia locus.
checks.explanation: The paper places GJA1 at 6q22-q23. The draft's 6q22.31 is the standard, more specific band within that range, so it counts as a chromosomal location restated in standard nomenclature.

paragraphs.text: Syndactyly type III is a limb malformation in which the ring and little fingers are joined (De Smet et al., 1994). Brachymesophalangia of the fifth finger is a frequent association (De Smet et al., 1994). McKiernan and McCann (1993) referred to familial syndactyly of the ring and little finger as type III syndactyly.

checks.claim: Syndactyly type III is a limb malformation in which the ring and little fingers are joined.
checks.evidence_quote: Five new cases of isolated syndactyly of the small and ring finger are described.
checks.explanation: The abstract describes syndactyly of the ring and small finger but never uses the term 'syndactyly type III' or defines it. That label comes from other sources.

checks.claim: Brachymesophalangia of the fifth finger is frequently associated with syndactyly type III.
checks.evidence_quote: Brachymesophalangia of the fifth finger is a frequent association.
checks.explanation: The abstract says this directly about ring and small finger syndactyly. Calling that condition 'type III' is the draft's own labelling.

checks.claim: McKiernan and McCann (1993) referred to familial syndactyly of the ring and little finger as type III syndactyly.
checks.evidence_quote: We present a pedigree containing 14 cases of familial syndactyly of the ring and little finger (Type III syndactyly).
checks.explanation: The abstract explicitly calls syndactyly of the ring and little finger Type III syndactyly.

paragraphs.text: Johnston and Kirby (1955) reported syndactyly of the ring and little finger.

checks.claim: Johnston and Kirby (1955) reported syndactyly of the ring and little finger.
checks.evidence_quote: Syndactyly of the ring and little finger.
checks.explanation: Only the title was supplied. It says the paper is about syndactyly of the ring and little finger, which matches the claim.

paragraphs.text: Brueton et al. (1990) regarded type III syndactyly as one of the characteristic findings of oculodentodigital dysplasia and asked whether oculodentodigital dysplasia and type III syndactyly are separate genetic entities or a disease spectrum.

checks.claim: Brueton et al. (1990) regarded type III syndactyly as one of the characteristic findings of oculodentodigital dysplasia.
checks.evidence_quote: A family is described with type III syndactyly and facies resembling the oculodentodigital dysplasia facial phenotype in the absence of any of the other characteristic findings of the latter condition.
checks.explanation: The wording 'other characteristic findings' shows the authors treat type III syndactyly as one of the characteristic findings of ODDD.

checks.claim: Brueton et al. (1990) asked whether oculodentodigital dysplasia and type III syndactyly are separate genetic entities or a disease spectrum.
checks.evidence_quote: Oculodentodigital dysplasia and type III syndactyly: separate genetic entities or disease spectrum?
checks.explanation: The paper's title asks exactly this question, and the abstract says the relationship between the two conditions is discussed.

paragraphs.text: Schrander-Stumpel et al. (1993) described a patient with complete cutaneous syndactyly of fingers 3 to 5 in the left hand and fingers 4 and 5 in the right hand.

checks.claim: Schrander-Stumpel et al. (1993) described a patient with complete cutaneous syndactyly of fingers 3 to 5 in the left hand.
checks.evidence_quote: A newborn male patient presented with complete cutaneous syndactyly of fingers 3-5 in the left hand
checks.explanation: The abstract says this directly.

checks.claim: The patient described by Schrander-Stumpel et al. (1993) had complete cutaneous syndactyly of fingers 4 and 5 in the right hand.
checks.evidence_quote: complete cutaneous syndactyly of fingers 3-5 in the left hand and fingers 4-5 in the right hand
checks.explanation: The abstract says this directly.

paragraphs.text: McKiernan and McCann (1993) reported familial syndactyly of the ring and little finger (type III syndactyly).

checks.claim: McKiernan and McCann (1993) reported familial syndactyly of the ring and little finger (type III syndactyly).
checks.evidence_quote: We present a pedigree containing 14 cases of familial syndactyly of the ring and little finger (Type III syndactyly).
checks.explanation: The abstract reports a family pedigree with this condition.

paragraphs.text: De Smet et al. (1994) described 5 new cases of isolated syndactyly of the small and ring finger. Brachymesophalangia of the fifth finger was a frequent association.

checks.claim: De Smet et al. (1994) described 5 new cases of isolated syndactyly of the small and ring finger.
checks.evidence_quote: Five new cases of isolated syndactyly of the small and ring finger are described.
checks.explanation: The abstract states this directly.

checks.claim: In the cases of isolated small and ring finger syndactyly described by De Smet et al. (1994), brachymesophalangia of the fifth finger was a frequent association.
checks.evidence_quote: Brachymesophalangia of the fifth finger is a frequent association.
checks.explanation: The abstract states this directly.

paragraphs.text: Paznekas et al. (2003) noted that oculodentodigital dysplasia presents with craniofacial (ocular, nasal, and dental) and limb dysmorphisms, and that syndactyly type III can occur in some cases.

checks.claim: Paznekas et al. (2003) noted that oculodentodigital dysplasia presents with craniofacial (ocular, nasal, and dental) dysmorphisms.
checks.evidence_quote: This autosomal dominant syndrome presents with craniofacial (ocular, nasal, and dental) and limb dysmorphisms
checks.explanation: The paper states this directly.

checks.claim: Paznekas et al. (2003) noted that oculodentodigital dysplasia presents with limb dysmorphisms.
checks.evidence_quote: This autosomal dominant syndrome presents with craniofacial (ocular, nasal, and dental) and limb dysmorphisms
checks.explanation: The paper states this directly.

checks.claim: Paznekas et al. (2003) noted that syndactyly type III can occur in some cases of oculodentodigital dysplasia.
checks.evidence_quote: Syndactyly type III and conductive deafness can occur in some cases
checks.explanation: The paper states this directly.

paragraphs.text: De Smet et al. (1994) stated that autosomal dominant inheritance of syndactyly type III was obvious.

checks.claim: De Smet et al. (1994) stated that autosomal dominant inheritance of syndactyly type III was obvious.
checks.evidence_quote: Autosomal dominant inheritance is obvious.
checks.explanation: The abstract states this about ring and small finger syndactyly, which the draft calls type III.

paragraphs.text: Paznekas et al. (2003) found that oculodentodigital dysplasia, in which type III syndactyly can occur, is caused by mutation in the GJA1 gene, which encodes connexin-43.

checks.claim: Paznekas et al. (2003) found that oculodentodigital dysplasia is caused by mutation in the GJA1 gene.
checks.evidence_quote: We found mutations in the GJA1 gene in all 17 families with oculodentodigital dysplasia that we screened.
checks.explanation: Supported by this sentence and by the title.

checks.claim: The GJA1 gene encodes connexin-43.
checks.evidence_quote: The human connexin 43 gene, or GJA1, is located at human chromosome 6q22-q23
checks.explanation: The paper identifies GJA1 as the connexin 43 gene.

checks.claim: Type III syndactyly can occur in oculodentodigital dysplasia.
checks.evidence_quote: Syndactyly type III and conductive deafness can occur in some cases
checks.explanation: The paper states this directly.

paragraphs.text: Richardson et al. (2004) reported that expression of Gja1 correlates with the phenotype observed in oculodentodigital syndrome/type III syndactyly.

checks.claim: Richardson et al. (2004) reported that expression of Gja1 correlates with the phenotype observed in oculodentodigital syndrome/type III syndactyly.
checks.evidence_quote: Expression of Gja1 correlates with the phenotype observed in oculodentodigital syndrome/type III syndactyly.
checks.explanation: The claim repeats the paper's title. Only the title was supplied, so no further detail could be checked.
